reading.translation:
While Socrates was speaking, the friends listened. He spoke about wisdom and sound self-control. It is not enough to know the good and do what is bad.

Socrates asks about freedom. When desires rule, is the person master of himself? For the slave of pleasure often fails to do what is best.

The self-controlled person can both learn and help friends. He does not take away every pleasure; he considers the right time and measure. In this way the argument leads toward life.

In a teaching example the teacher makes the boy stand. The boy stood and listened. When the speech ended, the boy went away. The same person does not perform every action.

Another example: the citizens appoint the man ruler. He then withdrew from office. The citizens appointed him, but he himself withdrew.

While the friends investigate, the discussion does not stop. Is self-mastery merely quietness, or a capacity to act well? We seek the answer in life and actions.

blocks.title: σωφροσύνη and ἐλευθερία
body: σωφροσύνη can include moderation, sound-mindedness, and self-control. It is broader than a single English label. ἐλευθερία names freedom; the argument asks what kind of freedom a person has when desires govern choices.
Keep the metaphorical and social senses visible. The word δοῦλος means an enslaved person; its use for subjection to appetite is a comparison within a society that also practiced actual slavery.

sections.title: 1. The genitive absolute
body: A genitive absolute supplies a circumstance with its own subject and participle, both in the genitive. τοῦ Σωκράτους λέγοντος means “while Socrates was speaking.” The phrase stands grammatically apart from the main clause: οἱ φίλοι ἤκουον, “the friends listened.”

The participle agrees with its own genitive subject, not the main subject. “Absolute” means detached in construction, not unconnected in meaning. Translate naturally as while, when, since, or although as context supports; do not choose cause automatically.

sections.title: 2. Participial aspect and shared subjects
body: A present participle normally shows action simultaneous with the main verb; an aorist participle normally presents a prior action. Thus λέγοντος may mean “while speaking,” and παυσαμένου “after it had ended.” The surrounding tense supplies the time frame.

When the participle describes the main subject, Greek normally uses an agreeing participle instead of a genitive absolute: ὁ φίλος λέγων ἔστη. Identify the people and relationships before translating.

sections.title: 3. ἵστημι: make stand or stand?
body: Present active ἵστημι is normally transitive, “make stand, set up.” Its first aorist ἔστησα also causes someone or something to stand. The second aorist ἔστην is intransitive, “I stood.” This difference is lexical and grammatical, not merely a change of time.
Learn the present ἵστημι, ἵστης, ἵστησι; ἵσταμεν, ἵστατε, ἱστᾶσι. Present middle ἵσταμαι commonly means “stand” or “take one’s stand”; perfect ἕστηκα has the present state sense “I am standing.”

sections.title: 4. καθίστημι and ἀφίστημι
body: Compounds retain the important causative/intransitive contrast. καθίστημι can mean “appoint” someone to a role; κατέστησα means “I appointed,” while κατέστην can mean “I became/was established.” An appointment often uses two accusatives: the person and the role.

ἀφίστημι can mean “make withdraw”; ἀπέστην means “I withdrew” or “revolted.” A genitive may express separation: ἀπέστη τῆς ἀρχῆς, “he withdrew from office.” Do not confuse ἀφίστημι with ἀφίημι, “release,” in the next lesson.

sections.title: Meet the Memorabilia: definitions tested by conduct
body: This lesson joins Memorabilia 3.9.4–5 with 4.5.1–12. In the first, Xenophon relates wisdom and self-control to knowing and doing what is good. In the second, Socrates examines the freedom lost when appetites govern conduct. These passages are related arguments, not one continuous ancient scene.

Think of the four books as a gallery of encounters rather than a continuous biography. Book 1 answers accusations against Socrates and presents his religious practice and daily conduct. Books 2–3 explore family, friendship, useful work, and leadership. Book 4 gives sustained attention to education, including the questioning of Euthydemus. The movement from an ordinary habit to a public responsibility is characteristic of the collection.

Xenophon writes as an advocate for a teacher condemned at Athens in 399 BCE. His Socrates improves other people through example, questions, and practical reasoning. That organizing purpose makes the work valuable evidence for an ancient interpretation of Socrates; it does not make every conversation a stenographic record. Notice who asks the questions, who changes position, and where the narrator supplies the judgment.

Reading invitation: open Book 1, chapter 5, then Book 4, chapter 5. Ask whether mastery of appetite is merely a rule about pleasure or a condition for learning and dependable action. Keep a small dossier of the different kinds of evidence Xenophon offers: reported speech, observed habit, analogy, and the narrator’s praise.

Across the module, the Memorabilia has offered habits, dialogue, allegory, and examination. Its variety serves Xenophon’s defense of Socrates as a useful teacher. You can now ask not only “What does Socrates say?” but also “How does Xenophon make this portrait persuasive?”

sections.title: Freedom as a capacity
body: In the argument, self-command makes learning, deliberating, and helping possible. Restraint is not merely the absence of visible movement. A person may sit quietly while being unable to attend to what matters.

Try the contrast with an ordinary task: putting off an interruption long enough to listen to a friend. What valuable action does restraint enable? Name that action rather than treating self-denial as its own reward.

sections.title: A metaphor with a social cost
body: Socrates’s language of being enslaved to pleasure draws force from a world where actual slavery existed. A metaphor of inner servitude should not make actual coerced labor disappear from view.

Distinguish the philosophical comparison from legal and social status. Someone can be legally enslaved regardless of personal self-control. Conversely, the argument can criticize the conduct of a legally free person. The two senses are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Build your definition with evidence
body: Choose two readings from the module that complicate one another: Socrates’s simple meal and the hungry army, or household order and the captive’s vulnerability. Write a definition of self-control broad enough to address both.

Attach one piece of evidence to each part of the definition. Then use a genitive absolute to set a circumstance and a finite verb to name a responsible action. Your final test is whether the definition guides conduct, not whether it sounds severe.

Compounds retain the important causative/intransitive contrast. καθίστημι can mean “appoint” someone to a role; κατέστησα means “I appointed,” while κατέστην can mean “I became/was established.” An appointment often uses two accusatives: the person and the role. ἀφίστημι can mean “make withdraw”; ἀπέστην means “I withdrew” or “revolted.” A genitive may express separation: ἀπέστη τῆς ἀρχῆς, “he withdrew from office.” Do not confuse ἀφίστημι with ἀφίημι, “release,” in the next lesson.
